title: How Could Iran Happen? An Autopsy.
gist: Tabatabai and Curlee argue the seventh-month U.S.-Israeli war on Iran — costing roughly $1 billion a day during heavy fighting — failed because Trump's institutional purges destroyed the planning capacity to run it: the NSC cut to under 50 policy experts, the Middle East senior director 12 days into the job with his team halved when strikes began, no contingency plan for Hormuz closure that decades of war games had predicted, and every major NATO ally refusing to send minesweepers.

themes.theme: War economics and the strategic outcome

insights.claim: The U.S.-Israeli campaign against Iran has run seven months with costs during periods of heavy fighting estimated at roughly $1 billion per day, versus Trump's promised 'four to five weeks.'
insights.speaker: Ariane Tabatabai, Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: A $1bn/day burn rate against an open-ended timeline is a direct fiscal and Treasury-supply consideration, and a driver of munitions replenishment orders.
insights.quote: with costs during periods of heavy fighting estimated at roughly $1 billion per day
insights.locator: The U.S.-Israeli campaign against Iran

insights.claim: Trump has traded maximalist objectives for terms inferior to the prewar status quo: a more hard-line Iranian regime still controls the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran — not the United States — now holds the upper hand in deciding when and on what terms the war ends.
insights.speaker: Ariane Tabatabai, Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: Tehran controls the timing of any de-escalation, meaning oil risk premia are set by Iranian rather than U.S. decisions — a critical asymmetry for energy positioning.
insights.quote: Iran now holds the upper hand in deciding when—and on what terms—the war ends
insights.locator: As the war dragged past his promised

insights.claim: Trump admitted within weeks of going to war that his administration did not foresee Iran closing the Strait of Hormuz, even though decades of war games had ended the same way — the White House simply underestimated Iran's willingness.
insights.speaker: Ariane Tabatabai, Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: The single most consequential energy-market event of the war was both predictable and unplanned for — a caution that official scenario planning is not a reliable guide to policy.
insights.locator: Within weeks of going to war

insights.claim: Every major NATO ally refused Trump's request to send minesweepers into the Strait of Hormuz to reopen it — the foreseeable cost of launching a war with no allied consultation.
insights.speaker: Ariane Tabatabai, Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: Allied refusal removes the most plausible path to reopening Hormuz at scale, extending the expected duration of the chokepoint disruption.
insights.quote: when the president later pressed European navies to send minesweepers into the Strait of Hormuz to reopen it, every major NATO ally refused
insights.locator: Likewise, the administration launched the war

insights.claim: U.S. military readiness has suffered from long deployments eroding morale, missed maintenance cycles and depleted munitions stocks, forcing the relocation of assets away from the priority Indo-Pacific theater.
insights.speaker: Ariane Tabatabai, Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: The Iran war is drawing capability away from the China contingency — raising Taiwan-scenario risk and guaranteeing multi-year munitions and maintenance appropriations.
insights.locator: Broader U.S. military readiness has also suffered

themes.theme: Institutional destruction as the causal mechanism

insights.claim: Three successive purges in January, April and May 2025 left the National Security Council with fewer than 50 policy experts — its smallest complement since the Eisenhower administration.
insights.speaker: Ariane Tabatabai, Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: Quantifies the loss of coordinating capacity at the center of U.S. national security — a structural reason to expect more unforced policy errors with market consequences.
insights.quote: This left the NSC with fewer than  50 policy experts, its smallest complement since the Eisenhower administration.
insights.locator: Since its creation, the National Security Council’s size

insights.claim: The senior director for Middle East policy was 12 days into the job when the June 2025 strikes on Iran's nuclear facilities began, with his team having just been cut from 10 officers to five.
insights.speaker: Ariane Tabatabai, Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: The specific staffing detail explains the planning failure — a five-person team twelve days in cannot run a regional war.
insights.locator: Since its creation, the National Security Council’s size

insights.claim: The White House chief of staff suspended the interagency meetings that new senior directors tried to restart, and the assistant-secretary-level cadence — where aspirations meet planning timelines, logistics and diplomacy — never resumed.
insights.speaker: Ariane Tabatabai, Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: Without interagency process, U.S. policy becomes discontinuous and improvised — raising the variance of policy outcomes that markets must price.
insights.locator: Initially, when the new senior directors

insights.claim: Having the secretary of state double as national security advisor produced uninformed decision-making and a lack of policy coordination, and a senior official told CNN that without the NSC as 'the final synthesizer' of options, 'the planning falls apart.'
insights.speaker: Ariane Tabatabai, Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: Dual-hatting the top two national security jobs removes the internal check on decisions — a structural feature that persists beyond this war.
insights.locator: A senior official later told CNN

insights.claim: The administration went to war having staged no charter flights and issued no departure advisories for the roughly half a million Americans living in the Middle East, advising departure only two days after strikes began when regional airspace had already closed — while Germany, France and the UK began evacuation plans within hours.
insights.speaker: Ariane Tabatabai, Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: Half a million exposed citizens with no evacuation plan is a live hostage and escalation risk that constrains U.S. options — and a corporate duty-of-care warning for firms with regional staff.
insights.locator: The administration was equally unprepared

insights.claim: Trump replaced first-term appointees like Gen. Jim Mattis with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a Fox News host whose military career ended at major and who had never led a policy-planning process or an institution approaching the Pentagon's scale.
insights.speaker: Ariane Tabatabai, Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: Leadership inexperience at the top of the Pentagon is a persistent source of execution risk in any future contingency, including Taiwan.
insights.locator: In his first term, Trump appointed seasoned professionals

insights.claim: Trump fired Joint Chiefs chairman Gen. Charles Q. Brown Jr. less than halfway into his term without stated cause, along with the chief of naval operations and the military's most senior lawyers, then elevated Gen. Dan Caine as a less-qualified officer seen as less willing to contradict him.
insights.speaker: Ariane Tabatabai, Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: Promotion now selects for compliance over candor at the top of the U.S. military — degrading the quality of military advice the president receives.
insights.quote: The officers who rose in the purged leaders’ places understood the terms of their promotions—and what candor with this president had cost their predecessors.
insights.locator: On assuming office, Trump’s team

insights.claim: With the workforce under perpetual threat of firing, Pentagon leadership at one point resorted to mass emailing staff for ideas on how to break the stalemate in the strait — tasks normally performed by policy arms in coordination with the NSC.
insights.speaker: Ariane Tabatabai, Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: A concrete indicator of how degraded U.S. planning capacity is — useful for calibrating expectations of any coherent Hormuz resolution.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, career civilians have been sidelined

insights.claim: Former officials who might testify to planning failures stay silent because silence is the price of employment at D.C.-area companies that do business with the government — suppressing the information flow that would normally surface such failures.
insights.speaker: Ariane Tabatabai, Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: Information about U.S. capability gaps is being systematically suppressed, meaning public assessments likely understate the problem.

themes.theme: Politicized intelligence and the broken feedback loop

insights.claim: This was not an intelligence failure like Iraq — the fault lies with policymakers who blocked warnings the president did not want to hear, with the administration's stated goal being to put career civil servants 'in trauma' so they would dread coming to work.
insights.speaker: Ariane Tabatabai, Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: Distinguishes collection failure from suppression — the latter is harder to fix and means future U.S. strategic surprises are more likely, not less.
insights.quote: the fault lies squarely with the policymakers who blocked the warnings that the president did not want to hear
insights.locator: Critics might dub Iran an intelligence failure

insights.claim: DNI Tulsi Gabbard politicized intelligence, gutted her own office and oversaw firings of officials who provided honest assessments reflecting intelligence community consensus, while the DIA director was fired before the war after his damage assessments of strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities undercut Trump's claims.
insights.speaker: Ariane Tabatabai, Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: Official U.S. damage assessments and threat claims about Iran should be treated as politically filtered — rely on independent verification for battle-damage and capability claims.
insights.locator: The more than a dozen agencies

insights.claim: When officers watch colleagues stripped of clearances and livelihoods for unwelcome conclusions, silence becomes automatic — 'a government that punishes warning gets none—and then blunders into crises that it forbade its analysts to predict.'
insights.speaker: Ariane Tabatabai, Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: A generalizable model of organizational blindness — applicable to any institution where forecasting is punished, and a reason to expect further U.S. strategic surprises.
insights.quote: A government that punishes warning gets none—and then blunders into crises that it forbade its analysts to predict.
insights.locator: This has flipped the intelligence-policy feedback loop

insights.claim: Trump has rarely read the President's Daily Brief or used intelligence to inform decisions, instead attacking agencies or assessments whose findings contradict his preferred narratives.
insights.speaker: Ariane Tabatabai, Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: Decisions are being made without the intelligence input markets implicitly assume exists — widening the distribution of possible U.S. policy actions.
insights.locator: Trump himself has rarely read

insights.claim: Congress enabled the outcome by failing to rein in Trump on war powers, doing nothing about the gutting of the NSC, and standing by as generals and admirals were purged, even while administration officials stonewalled hearings while requesting increased war appropriations.
insights.speaker: Ariane Tabatabai, Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: No institutional brake exists on war duration or cost — remove congressional constraint from any model of when the Iran war ends.
insights.locator: None of the above would have been possible

insights.claim: The Iran war functioned as a stress test proving that complex institutions require expert professionals — cutting government for its own sake left the state without the expertise to plan, execute or end a major war.
insights.speaker: Ariane Tabatabai, Julia Curlee
insights.so_what: State capacity is a priced variable: its erosion raises the cost and duration of every subsequent crisis the U.S. faces.
insights.quote: It is what happens when a government fires its air traffic controllers and expects the planes to land themselves.
insights.locator: The war in Iran was a stress test
